newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hanbo founder seeks to suspend auction.
newsitem.headline: Hanbo founder seeks to suspend auction.

text.p: The jailed founder of South Korea's troubled Hanbo Group has asked creditors to stop the auction of its failed steelmaker and suggested he could run the company, the Korea First Bank said on Friday.

"I hope your bank and creditors agree to our request to withdraw the application to liquidate the company and to halt the auction aimed at finding a third party to take over the company," chairman Chung Tae-soo said.
Chung's request was delivered by his lawyer in a letter to the Korea First Bank, Hanbo's main creditor.
"I ask you to let both me and the company complete the construction," Chung said. The facility is about 90 percent complete.
A Korea First Bank official called Chung "shameless" and his proposal "ridiculous". "How can Chung, who gave a serious blow to the nation's economy and is in jail for this, demand it?"
"His request is not even worth considering," he added.

The January collapse of Hanbo Steel Co, declared insolvent after piling up some $5.8 billion in debt, rocked South Korea's economy. The loans-for-kickback scandal uncovered a web of corruption involving top bankers and politicians.
Hanbo Steel has been constructing a steel mill in Tangjin, 80 km southwest of Seoul, which if completed would raise Hanbo's steel production capability to six million tonnes annually.
In his letter to Korea First Bank, Chung said: "I will accept all the conditions offered by creditors to take over the steelmaker."
The first auction slated for July 8 to sell off the flagship unit of the nation's 14th largest conglomerate ended with no offers submitted.
Creditors re-scheduled the auction for July 29. The outcome was expected to be announced on August 1.
Analysts said the sale would not be easily achieved unless creditors improved their takeover terms.
Potential buyers have been asked to indicate their going-concern value of Hanbo Steel as well as how much of the steelmaker's liabilities and assets they will assume.
An accounting company commissioned to evaluate the steelmaker estimated its liabilities at 6.61 trillion won, compared to assets of 4.97 trillion.
Hanbo had said its assets totalled 8.7 trillion won.

The buyer of Hanbo Steel would repay the liabilities over five years after a 10-year grace period. Annual interest on the liabilities would be 8.5 percent during the grace period and 11.5 percent thereafter.
The buyer also must detail a plan to raise capital.

"I think my way will ensure that creditors will not be damaged and the company can survive. And I believe it will greatly contribute to the nation's economy," Chung said. "It will be the last opportunity for me to devote myself to the nation's industrial prosperity," he added.
